diagnosis.question: why was every HydraDB request ~45 ms, flat from 100 to 5,000 services?
diagnosis.cause: Per-request overhead in the client-to-published-port hop, not HydraDB and not graph work. HydraDB answers in 0.1 to 0.9 ms (server-side, from its /metrics histogram) and its response always arrives in one read. Clients that write the request headers and body separately (httpx, http.client, HTTP/2) took ~45 ms through Docker Desktop's published port on Windows; the same clients inside the docker network took 0.3 to 1.5 ms. A client that sends headers+body in ONE write took 0.4 ms through the same published port, and so did Bolt. Client-side TCP_NODELAY did not change it (so it is not simply the client's Nagle), which points at the proxy hop reacting to the split writes.
diagnosis.server_response_writes: 1 read per response (no header/body split), max gap between reads 0 ms
diagnosis.response_timing_fields: none in the HTTP response (columns, rows, read_epoch, next_cursor, bookmark); server timing comes from /metrics graph_client_operation_read_duration_seconds
diagnosis.transport_chosen: persistent HTTP/1.1 connection, one write per request (ghostwalk/graph/fasthttp.py): identical results (8 parity tests), 0.5 ms vs 45 ms per query; Bolt (~1 ms) was the alternative
also_fixed: the revision check is id-anchored (about 1 ms instead of 12 ms)
a graph read issues its independent queries together (about 40 ms instead of 85 ms)
diagnosis.not_transport: HydraDB writes still take about 22 ms each (server-side commit), and a scan filtered on a property such as `co` costs 11 to 50 ms server-side

hydradb.status: not run at scale: HydraDB is reachable, but a write costs about 65 ms (one request per edge), so loading 1,000 or 5,000 services through it was not benchmarked. Its latency on the 30 TEST companies is in ops.hydradb_latency

gate.rule: stop if p95 at 1,000 services < 100 ms; port walk()'s Bellman-Ford to Rust only if p95 at 5,000 services > 250 ms

hygiene: adjacency built once per graph revision and cached (GraphState.invalidate on every learner write)

HydraDB path costs (-ln w) are already stored with w on every write; UNWIND batching of path queries was NOT done (needs a node and a response parser)
no per-request JSON reload: results.json is re-read only when its mtime changes

definitions.hit@5: a retrieved past incident has the same root cause as the current one; defined only for repeat incidents (a past incident with that root exists)
definitions.mrr: 1 / rank of the first same-root past incident in the top 5, else 0 (repeat incidents)
definitions.related@5: a retrieved past incident whose true causal chain shares a dependency edge with the current incident's chain (used for novel incidents, where hit@5 cannot exist)
definitions.graph: HydraDB traversal: past incidents with an alert on a service within 2 hops of the alerting services, ranked by neighbourhood overlap; alert text unused
definitions.vector: pgvector: nearest 5 past postmortems to the embedded alert text (feature-hashing bag-of-words, 512 dims)
definitions.keyword: TF-IDF cosine between the alert text and past postmortem texts

$ gw why-edge experiment-svc ledger-db

  experiment-svc -> ledger-db   w 0.70  learned  2 confirmations

  lesson L153  confirmed  w 0.70  created at revision 4
    taught by   INC-1004  root ledger-db  path experiment-svc -> ledger-db
    confirmed   ✓ INC-1018

persistence.killed: the API process (kill -9) and its state file
persistence.summary: Twenty incidents were learned through the API with GW_STORE=hydradb; the API process was killed and its state file deleted; a new process re-attached to HydraDB and ranked incident 21 identically (all 5 candidates, names and confidences) (`scripts/persistence_demo.py`, transcript in `docs/measurements/persistence_demo.txt`). The same holds in a test that also compares against the in-memory learner.
